title: How would you calculate the availability of this system end-to-end?
summary: Tests whether you can chain component availabilities correctly — multiply for serial dependencies, use redundancy math for parallel ones — instead of quoting "five nines" with no arithmetic behind it.

slides.markdown:
"What's the availability of this system?" sounds like a trivia question, but interviewers ask it to see if you'll actually do the arithmetic instead of reciting "99.99%" as a slogan. Availability chains: **multiply** component availabilities along a serial path, and use **redundancy math** for parallel, replicated paths.

By the end of this topic you'll be able to chain a real system's numbers end-to-end and know exactly which component to improve first.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: which components are on the critical path?
slides.markdown:
Before multiplying anything, separate what's actually **on the critical path** — required for the request to succeed — from what's **optional or best-effort**, like a recommendation widget that can fail silently without failing the whole request.

Only critical-path components enter the availability calculation. Including an optional dependency you'd actually degrade gracefully around would understate the system's real availability.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: multiply serial, redundancy-math parallel
slides.markdown:
The skeleton: for components a request must pass through **in sequence** (serial dependencies), multiply their availabilities together — the chain is only as available as the product of its links. For components that are **redundant copies** of the same thing (parallel paths, like two DB replicas), use `1-(1-p)^n`, since the path only fails if *all* n copies fail simultaneously.

Getting these two formulas right, and applying the correct one to each part of the diagram, is what this question is actually testing.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a worked serial chain
slides.markdown:
A request passes through a load balancer (99.99%), an app server (99.95%), and a database (99.9%) in sequence. Multiply them:

```
0.9999 * 0.9995 * 0.999 = 0.99830...  ≈ 99.83%
```

Notice the chain's availability (99.83%) is *lower* than every individual component — that's the cost of a serial dependency. Each additional hop on the critical path drags the whole number down, even if every hop is individually solid.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: adding a redundant replica
slides.markdown:
Say the database in that chain is only 90% available on its own (a rough single-node number). Adding one redundant replica turns it from a serial single point into a parallel pair:

```
1 - (1 - 0.1)^2 = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99  → 99% availability for the DB tier
```

Two unreliable nodes in parallel can beat one very reliable node, because the pair only fails if *both* fail at once — which is why redundancy, not just "buy a better box," is usually the fastest way to raise a weak link's number.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: turning the percentage into minutes of downtime
slides.markdown:
A percentage means little until it's minutes. For a 30-day month (43,200 minutes):

```
99.83% availability  ->  (1 - 0.9983) * 43200 ≈ 73 minutes of downtime/month
99.9%  availability  ->  (1 - 0.999)  * 43200 ≈ 43 minutes of downtime/month
99.99% availability  ->  (1 - 0.9999) * 43200 ≈ 4.3 minutes of downtime/month
```

Saying "that's about an hour of downtime a month" instead of "99.83%" is what makes the number land with a business stakeholder — and it's the detail interviewers want to see you reach for.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a third-party dependency caps your ceiling
slides.markdown:
If a payments API you call is contractually rated at 99.9% availability and it's on the critical path for checkout, your system's checkout availability **cannot exceed 99.9%**, no matter how well you build everything else — the chain's ceiling is set by its worst serial link.

This is worth naming explicitly: it shows you understand availability math isn't just about your own infrastructure, and it sets honest expectations for what an SLA commitment can actually promise.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: every extra nine costs real effort
slides.markdown:
| Availability | Downtime/month | Typical engineering cost to reach it |
|---|---|---|
| 99% | ~7.3 hours | Single instance, manual restarts |
| 99.9% | ~43 minutes | Basic redundancy, automated restarts |
| 99.99% | ~4.3 minutes | Multi-AZ, automated failover, on-call |
| 99.999% | ~26 seconds | Multi-region, extensive automation, large team |

**How to decide:** each additional nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more engineering effort than the last — name the business cost of downtime at the current tier before proposing the next one.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: which component should you improve first?
slides.markdown:
Improve the **lowest-availability link that's on the critical path** — it has the most leverage, since the chain's total availability is bounded by its weakest link, not its average.

In the worked example, the database at 99.9% was the weakest serial link; fixing it with a replica pair had far more impact on the end-to-end number than shaving the already-strong load balancer from 99.99% to 99.995%.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does retrying a failed call change this math?
slides.markdown:
Yes — **retries raise effective availability** for transient failures, since a retried call that succeeds counts as success even though the first attempt failed. If a dependency is 99% available per attempt and failures are independent, two attempts push effective success close to `1 - (1-0.99)^2 ≈ 99.99%`.

The cost: retries add latency (you pay for the failed attempt's timeout before the retry succeeds) and can amplify load on an already-struggling dependency — say both trade-offs, not just the availability win.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: quoting 99.99% with no math behind it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We'll target 99.99% availability" is a sufficient answer because it's the number everyone quotes.

**Why it's wrong:** without chaining the actual component numbers, this is a slogan, not an engineering claim — an interviewer who asks you to show the math will immediately expose that the number was never computed. A single weak serial dependency, even one you don't own, can make 99.99% mathematically impossible.

**Correct model:** always be ready to chain the real numbers — serial multiplication, redundancy math for parallel paths — and state the resulting number, not the aspirational one.

If you only have a minute: identify the critical-path components, multiply serial availabilities and apply `1-(1-p)^n` for redundant parallel ones, then convert the result into minutes of downtime/month so it means something to a stakeholder.

Name the weakest link — including any third-party dependency — as the one worth improving first, and mention that every additional nine costs roughly an order of magnitude more effort. This builds on [availability and reliability](availability-and-reliability).
